extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in liberal political philosophy and the limits of state/social authority
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding when society or law may legitimately interfere with individual conduct, distinguishing self-regarding acts from acts that harm others, and evaluating the proper roles of persuasion, opinion, and legal coercion. Useful for analyzing public policy, moral legislation, and debates about liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person's conduct affects no persons besides himself (and need not affect them unless they like), 'there should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society has no jurisdiction where conduct concerns only the actor (assuming full age and ordinary understanding). Such self-regarding acts should be left to individual spontaneity; interference requires special justification. Examples/explanations: full quotation: 'In all such cases there should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal enforcement of rights and mutual obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is justified in enforcing conditions that concern rights and each person's bearing his share (to be fixed on some equitable principle) of the labours and sacrifices incurred for defending the society or its members from injury and molestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conditions may be enforced 'at all costs to those who endeavour to withhold fulfilment.' This identifies a class of social rules that legitimately fall within legal coercion: protection of rights and enforcement of equitable contributions to common defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion (social sanction) v. legal punishment for non-rights-violating harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that are hurtful or wanting in due consideration for others' welfare but do not violate constituted rights may be 'justly punished by opinion though not by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conduct harms feelings or is inconsiderate without breaching legal rights, social reprobation, ostracism, or withholding of favors is appropriate, whereas legal penalties are not. The text contrasts these social penalties with punishments that are matters for law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference justified where conduct prejudicially affects others or risks definite damage
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction; whenever there is a definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, the case is taken out of the province of liberty and placed in that of morality or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operational test: presence of definite harm or definite risk to others brings conduct within permissible regulation or punishment. The 'general welfare' question becomes open once others' interests are prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and persuasion rather than compulsion for cultivating self-regarding virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should cultivate both social and self-regarding virtues, but 'it is by [conviction and persuasion] only that, when the period of education is past, the self-regarding virtues should be inculcated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use persuasion and other non-coercive instruments rather than 'whips and scourges' (literal or metaphorical) to shape private conduct. Coercion undermines individuality and may provoke rebellion among independent characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual as final judge of his own concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual 'is the person most interested in his own well-being' and 'he himself is the final judge.' Interference to overrule his judgment must rest on general presumptions, which may be wrong or misapplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because others lack the knowledge of an individual's circumstances, their presumptions about his good are likely misapplied. This is a reason for deference to individual choice in matters that concern only the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible social reactions short of coercion (avoidance, warning, preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: We have rights to act on unfavourable opinions—'we are not bound... to seek his society; we have a right to avoid it... We may give others a preference over him in optional good offices... We may give caution to others against him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural consequences such as social avoidance, withholding of optional favors, and warning others are acceptable responses to private faults, but they are not to be treated as deliberate punishments imposed by society; they are the spontaneous outcomes of reputation and choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts injurious to others merit moral reprobation and possibly legal punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Encroachment on others' rights, infliction of loss or damage, falsehood, unfair or ungenerous exploitation, and selfish abstinence from defending others are 'fit objects of moral reprobation, and, in grave cases, of moral retribution and punishment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not only harmful acts but the dispositions that lead to them (cruelty, malice, envy, dissimulation, domineering desire, etc.) are morally culpable. Such conduct falls properly within social condemnation and, where serious, legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to oneself are not socially obligatory unless they become duties to others
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called duties to ourselves are not socially obligatory, unless circumstances render them at the same time duties to others; 'the term duty to oneself... means self-respect or self-development' for which one is not accountable to fellow-creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private obligations (prudence, self-improvement) do not justify social or legal compulsion unless failure to meet them injures others or neglects an obligation owed to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between private imprudence and social offence should determine response
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconveniences inseparable from unfavourable judgment of others are the only ones a person should suffer for conduct that concerns only his own good and does not affect others' interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conduct only harms the actor, others should aim to alleviate rather than aggravate his punishment; feelings of pity or dislike are appropriate, but anger, resentment, or deliberate making of his life uncomfortable are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society's obligation to educate and not abandon those unfit for self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has had absolute power over children and the early period of life to try to make them capable of rational conduct; 'the existing generation is master both of the training and the entire circumstances of the generation to come.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society must use education, authoritative opinion, and social influence to cultivate capacities for self-government; failure to do so makes society responsible for subsequent incapacity and does not justify later coercion of adults as if society bore no prior role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is an unreliable basis for coercion in self-regarding matters
rubrics_metrics.description: On self-regarding conduct, 'the opinion of the public... is quite as likely to be wrong as right' because public judgment often reflects tastes and preferences rather than accurate assessments of others' good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law grounded in majority tastes risks imposing arbitrary standards; the public often enforces conformity to its feelings rather than to reasoned interests. This is a caution against letting moral majorities legislate private conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expansion of 'moral police'—majority imposition of private tastes as law
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend the bounds of what may be called moral police until it encroaches on legitimate liberty is a universal propensity; examples include imposing religious observances, banning amusements, sumptuary expectations, and enforcing modes of worship or dress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that many moralists present personal feelings as universal moral laws makes public censorship likely and illegitimate in many cases. The text supplies historical and contemporary examples (Puritans, Sabbatarianism, social pressure in democratic societies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal restrictions are permissible only to protect direct interests of others (limited justification for Sabbath laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstinence on one day (Sabbath) may be justifiable insofar as the law guarantees observance because some people's work imposes on others; but this justification 'does not apply to the self-chosen occupations... nor does it hold good... for legal restrictions on amusements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law can legitimate constraints when one person's leisure imposes costs on others (e.g., the need for a common day of rest affecting workers), but it should not extend to prohibiting voluntary amusements or leisure that do not injure others' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'social rights' that claim a right to others' moral or material conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every individual has an absolute social right that every other individual 'shall act in every respect exactly as he ought' is 'monstrous' and would justify any interference with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation should not be based on a notion that the public has a vested interest in each other's moral, intellectual, or physical perfection defined by each claimant. Such a principle annihilates freedom and legitimizes persecutory enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward prohibitory legislation based on diffuse social-cost claims (e.g., alcohol prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws that prohibit private consumption (prohibition of fermented drinks) are suspect when they interfere with acts that are properly individual; the Secretary's claim that the traffic in strong drink invades social rights is critiqued as overbroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between regulating trade/social acts (selling liquor as a social act) and criminalizing personal consumption. Be wary of arguments that treat every private vice as a ground for legal prohibition by invoking supposed harms to social security, equality, or moral development.
